prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: Reading the full set of opening ballots, B013 is the candidate on which the committee's independent assessments converge most. All eight members ranked it, four placed it in their top three, and two ranked it first. My own opening ranked it only fourth, but my ranking was dominated by circuit QED, which I know best and which I now think is the wrong candidate for me to push. On substance, the magic-wavelength lattice removes the Stark and motional shifts while keeping the statistical power of many atoms. That is a clean idea, with a clean attribution to Katori for the concept and Ye for pushing accuracy and stability to the 10^-18 regime. The results have been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, which is exactly the robustness across laboratories that I look for. The discovery is a new regime of measurement, with direct reach into tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. A two-person prize is natural and avoids the credit problems that afflict several other entries.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize may be read as an instrument and metrology achievement rather than the discovery of a new physical phenomenon, and that it sits next to work already honoured in 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (ion trapping and cavity QED), so the marginal novelty must be argued carefully. The headline physics payoff, such as a dark-sector or varying-constant signal, has not yet arrived, and the redefinition of the second is still pending. Lattice clocks also owe a great deal to a wider community (Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Takamoto and others) whom a two-name prize leaves out.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B013 first as an instrument that changes what can be measured: 10^-18 uncertainty, tens of times better than microwave standards, with Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy and many-body work both well supported.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and the reproducibility argument. Where I would qualify it is the phrase 'changes what can be measured'. I think the citation should stay anchored to the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at 10^-18, not to future applications such as geodesy or the second, because the committee rewards a demonstrated achievement, not the promise. I would also ask that we note openly that the redefinition of the second is still pending, so the prize is timely but does not depend on it.

responses.point: Lindroth values B013 as a quantitative precision result with hard numbers, building on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstration of 10^-18 systematic uncertainty, and she notes that the 2012 prize covered ion trapping and cavity QED.
responses.response: I largely share this view and defer to her on atomic structure. I would add that the 2012 prize and the 2005 comb prize concern different things from the lattice clock: the lattice gives many-atom statistics with a controlled systematic, which the ion clocks do not. The overlap concern is therefore real but answerable. We should still be careful in the citation not to claim credit for the comb or for single-ion clocks.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B034 (Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase) first, as a unifying concept with enormous cross-disciplinary reach, a simple universal mechanism and a recognition that is arguably overdue, with age a practical consideration.
responses.response: I accept the conceptual depth and that Berry phases underlie much of modern topological physics, so I rank B034 highly on merit. My concerns are priority and attribution: Mehlig himself lists Pancharatnam, Ehrenberg-Siday, Mead-Truhlar and Simon, and Bohm cannot share the prize. Overdue is not by itself an argument for the most defensible configuration this year. I would keep B034 as a serious runner-up for a future year, and I do not put it in my alternatives only because I think B001 and B048 have cleaner credit lines.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B035) first because nature supplied the clue: a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, with the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 evidence, opening neutrino astronomy.
responses.response: I defer to him on astroparticle physics and I agree that a window opened by nature is a strong kind of discovery. My reservation is the one he raises himself: source identification rests on a few objects at several sigma, and the credit for a collaboration of this size is not clean with two names. I would rather see that picture firm up before a prize. I also note that he ranks B013 second, so there may be common ground.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the topological insulator candidate (B048) first as a genuinely new quantum state of matter, but concedes that the omission of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction is a fairness concern.
responses.response: I think that concern is serious. Without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, the HgTe experiment by Molenkamp's group is not fully explained by the credited names, and Zhang's death complicates any repair. Mehlig also points out that the 2016 topological-phases prize makes the marginal recognition harder to argue. For those reasons I keep B048 only as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a precision-measurement and instrument achievement as sufficiently a discovery, given the earlier 2005 and 2012 prizes nearby.
Whether leaving out other lattice-clock contributors (Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Takamoto and others) is acceptable under the three-person limit.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second, or a future fundamental-physics result from clocks, would make the timing better or worse a few years from now.
I am unable to judge astrophysical, topological-materials and electron-optics candidates at the same depth as quantum optics and circuits.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits and circuit QED, and WACQT colleagues include Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson. That is a real connection to B008, which I ranked first in my opening, so I should recuse myself from any decision that centres on B008. For B013 and the other shortlisted entries no specific personal or institutional connection is apparent from my profile.
